## Apple FaceID, TouchID, SEP

* Application Processor (AP) versus Secure Enclave Processor (SEP).
* The *Secure Enclave* is similar to Arm TrustZone.
* It is hardware-based isolation.
* Biometrics and keys are only handled by the SEP.
* There is a specific interface between the AP and the SEP.

# Confinement

## Run Untrusted Code

* Apps, plugins, codecs.
* Software not written by you, not verified.
* Damage control.
* Kill it if it misbehaves.
* Ensure a misbehaving app does not alter the system.

## Confinement Types

* hardware: different hardware systems, air gap
* virtual machine: isolate OSes in a single machine
* process: sandboxing, jailing
* application: software fault isolation

## Software Fault Isolation

* Isolate components in their *fault domain*.
* The components are part of the same address space.
* It requires some OS or hardware support to separate addresses.
* Mogoșanu et al.: MicroStache: A Lightweight Execution Context for In-Process Safe Region Isolation.

## Reference Monitor

* It mediates requests, implements policy, and enforces isolation and confinement.
* It must always be invoked.
* It must be tamperproof.
* It must be validated.

# System Isolation. Trusted Computing Base

## Principles and Goals

* least privilege
* privilege separation
* safely execute a non-trusted program
* harden a system that runs programs that increase its attack surface
* isolate what can happen if a vulnerability is exploited

## Mechanism and Policy

* mechanism: how goals are achieved
* policy: rules that achieve isolation goals
* mechanism: mostly implementation
* policy: mostly configuration

## Mechanisms and Policies

> **TODO (figure):** isolation mechanisms and policies (source: Rui Shu et al., A Study of Security Isolation Techniques) — from slides.tex

## System Isolation

* Isolate an app, a group of apps, or an entire OS.
* Prevent it from hurting other components.
* Mechanisms: virtual machines, library OS, containers.
* We consider sandboxing, mandatory access control, and software fault isolation (SFI) to be app-centric mechanisms (not system-centric).

## Trusted Computing Base (TCB)

* The TCB holds the system components trusted by the reference monitor.
* These are the critical parts of the system.
* If exploited, they might jeopardize the security of the entire system.
* The TCB is aimed to be small (reduced attack surface).

# Hardware Components

## Hardware Protection

* Hardware provides security isolation for shared resources.
* Passive components: TPM (*Trusted Platform Module*).
* Active components: control critical system operations.

## Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)

* A TEE is a secure area on the CPU.
* The code that runs in it is secure: confidentiality and integrity.
* It runs in parallel with the OS.

## TEE (2)

> **TODO (figure):** normal world versus secure world (source: infosecinstitute, understanding iOS security) — from slides.tex

## Intel TXT

* Trusted eXecution Technology.
* It attests the platform and operating system.
* It uses the TPM and cryptography to validate and measure code that can be trusted.

## Arm TrustZone

* Arm TZ.
* There are two worlds: secure and non-secure.
* The rich OS runs in the non-secure world, security-specialized code in the secure world.
* The aim is to reduce the attack surface.

## Arm TrustZone (2)

> **TODO (figure):** Arm TrustZone secure and non-secure worlds (source: Quarkslab) — from slides.tex

## Intel SGX

* Software Guard eXtensions.
* Specialized instructions.
* User-level code allocates enclaves.
* Enclaves are protected from higher privilege level components.
* Use case: secure remote computation.
* Weakness: cache and DRAM side-channel attacks.

## Secure Enclave

* It is found on Apple iOS and watchOS devices.
* Fingerprint data is completely walled off from the OS.
* It uses a SEP (*Secure Enclave Processor*) and a SEP OS.
* It is based on Arm TZ.

# Virtualization

## Virtualization

> **TODO (figure):** virtualization (source: Rui Shu et al., A Study of Security Isolation Techniques) — from slides.tex

## Virtual Machine

* A VM runs an isolated OS instance on top of a supervisor component (hypervisor).
* The supervisor is the hypervisor or VMM (*Virtual Machine Monitor*).
* Malware in a VM cannot infect the host OS or other VMs.

## Covert Channels

* Side channels.
* They use CPU, memory, and cache information from one VM to determine what is happening on the other VM.

## VMM Detection

* VM platforms emulate simple hardware.
* The VMM introduces time latency variances.
* The VMM shares the TLB (*Translation Lookaside Buffers*).

## Type-1 vs Type-2

* Type-2: additional flexibility.
* Type-1: reduced TCB.
* Type-1: efficiency.

# Library OS

## Library OS

> **TODO (figure):** library OS (source: Rui Shu et al., A Study of Security Isolation Techniques) — from slides.tex

## Library OS Characteristics

* Also called a unikernel.
* OS functionality is provided as user library or libraries.
* It is a single-image app that can run on top of a hypervisor or hardware.
* There is no need for user-level/kernel-level transitions.
* It is difficult to run multiple instances: use a hypervisor.
* It reduces the attack surface.

## Implementations

* ClickOS: virtualized software middle box.
* LKL (*Linux Kernel Library*).
* [My VM is Lighter (and Safer) than Your Container](http://cnp.neclab.eu/projects/lightvm/lightvm.pdf)

# Containerization

## Containers

> **TODO (figure):** containers (source: Rui Shu et al., A Study of Security Isolation Techniques) — from slides.tex

## Container

* A container is a restricted environment.
* It holds applications or application groups.
* Sandboxing only provides a certain set of privileges.
* Containers provide a dedicated isolated environment.

## LXC/Docker

* LXC: Linux Containers.
* They use Linux namespaces: PID, network, IPC, mount, user, UTS.
* Linux control groups (cgroups) limit, account, and isolate resource usage.

## OS vs. Application Containers

* OS containers provide an entire distro, similar to a virtual machine (LXC).
* Application containers provide an environment for running a single service (Docker).

## Containers vs. hypervisors

* Containers are faster to create, deploy, and run.
* Containers are lighter (reduced overhead).
* Hypervisors are more secure: reduced TCB, no common kernel.
